reference.source: Cardiology references / acute coronary syndrome literature
clinicalPearls: A mechanical complication of acute myocardial infarction causing sudden severe mitral regurgitation
It typically occurs a few days after infarction and presents with abrupt pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock
The posteromedial papillary muscle is more vulnerable because it has a single coronary blood supply
The murmur may be soft or absent despite severe regurgitation because of rapid pressure equalisation
Echocardiography (often transoesophageal) is diagnostic, showing a flail leaflet and severe regurgitation
It is a surgical emergency; temporising measures include afterload reduction and mechanical circulatory support
reference.pathophysiology: Papillary muscle rupture results from ischaemic necrosis of a papillary muscle following myocardial infarction, most often affecting the posteromedial muscle owing to its single-vessel supply. Complete or partial rupture disrupts the subvalvular apparatus, producing an acutely flail mitral leaflet and torrential mitral regurgitation. Because the left atrium and ventricle cannot accommodate the sudden volume, pressures equalise rapidly, causing flash pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock, and the murmur may therefore be unimpressive despite catastrophic haemodynamics.
additionalDifferentials: Acute ischaemic mitral regurgitation without rupture
Spontaneous chordal rupture in degenerative valve disease
additionalInvestigations: Electrocardiogram and cardiac biomarkers confirming infarction
redFlags: Acute pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock after recent infarction
A new severe mitral regurgitation, even with a soft murmur
reference.prognosis: Without surgery mortality is very high; emergency valve surgery, supported by mechanical circulatory support and revascularisation, offers the best chance of survival though operative risk is substantial.
pitfalls: Being falsely reassured by a soft or absent murmur
Confusing it with post-infarction ventricular septal rupture
Delaying surgery in a deteriorating patient
Attributing shock solely to left ventricular dysfunction
management: Emergency mitral valve replacement or repair is the definitive treatment and should not be delayed
Afterload reduction with intravenous vasodilators such as sodium nitroprusside to lower the regurgitant fraction as a temporising measure
Mechanical circulatory support with intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation, or a short-term ventricular assist device or ECMO, to stabilise cardiogenic shock before theatre
Concurrent coronary revascularisation by surgical grafting or percutaneous intervention to treat the underlying infarction
Supportive intensive care with positive-pressure ventilation and diuresis for flash pulmonary oedema, with cautious inotropic support
Continuous invasive haemodynamic and transoesophageal echocardiographic monitoring within a heart-team and cardiac-surgical setting
